summary: Sustained pipeline lag in dedicated pool triggered by burst of small-tenant cold-starts
description:
Issue summary:
Customer reports sustained p99/p95 latency regression in their dedicated GPU pool that coincided with a sudden increase in many very short-lived streaming requests from several of their microservices. The behaviour started ~2026-03-12T09:15 UTC and persisted for multiple hours with intermittent recoveries.

Impact:
- Affected customer: Acme AI (dedicated).
- Visible degradation: p99 latency increased from ~220ms to 900-1,500ms for text generation routes; throughput dropped ~18% on the dedicated pool.
- Error rate: no large spike in 5xx; a small increase in 429s for burst limits on some routes.

Environment:
- prod | us-west-2 dedicated pool (pool id: ded-usw2-37).
- Models: redwood-open-7b (primary), redwood-compat-2.7b-quant (fallback).

Steps to reproduce (best-effort):
1) Send a high fanout of short, streaming requests (avg latency per request < 200ms, request tokens < 30) across many client connections.
2) Observe that autoscaler issues several low-granularity GPU slot allocations; KV/prefix cache is frequently cold.
3) The serving runtime shows lower batch sizes and elevated kernel warmup counts.

Observed metrics and logs (links):
- Console: per-model p99 latency: https://console.redwood.ai/dedicated/pool/ded-usw2-37/latency (redacted).
- Autoscaler events: burst of 1-2 slot allocations per minute for ~45 mins starting 09:16 UTC.
- Serving runtime logs: repeated small-batch execution traces and frequent "kernel_warmup" entries.
- GPU metrics: sustained lower utilization (30-45%) with higher context-switches and PCIe stalls.

Investigation notes / hypotheses so far:
- Hypothesis A: Cold-start flood from many small short-lived streams prevents batching from forming, causing per-token overhead to dominate and kernel warmups to amplify p99 latency.
- Hypothesis B: Slot fragmentation (many tiny allocations) prevents the runtime from consolidating streams into efficient batches; aggressive autoscale policy is adding/removing slots too quickly.
- Hypothesis C: A single tenant in the pool (Acme AI microservice cluster) has many ephemeral clients causing noisy-neighbor like resource churn; not classical noisy-tenant CPU/GPU hogs but allocation churn.

Immediate mitigations applied:
- SRE increased short-term batching window (trial) to 25ms for affected routes to allow more micro-batches to coalesce (rollout at 09:42 UTC).
- Applied a temporary autoscaler debounce: min-stable-window increased from 30s -> 90s for ded-usw2-37 (09:50 UTC) to reduce thrashing.
- Enabled per-route rate-limiting advisory to the customer (support provided rate-limit recommendations).

Partial findings:
- After increasing batching window, average batch size increased from 1.6 -> 3.8 and p99 improved ~30% but did not fully return to baseline; throughput remained ~10% below baseline.
- Debounce reduced allocation churn; however, some GPU slots remained underutilized due to many short streams that immediately closed after a few tokens.
- Kernel warmup counts reduced but persisted for requests hitting the quantized model variant.

Workarounds shared with customer:
- Consolidate client-side connections: recommend connection pooling and keepalives instead of many ephemeral short-lived streams.
- Use a dedicated long-lived worker for high-fanout jobs to amortize cold starts.
- Pin heavier requests to the larger model endpoint to reduce cross-model fallbacks.

Next steps / follow-ups:
- SRE: run deeper trace to identify whether a specific microservice in Acme's fleet is responsible for >60% of the short streams (assigned Marco Ruiz).
- Infra: evaluate autoscaler policy options across small-allocation clustering and aggressive consolidation heuristics (follow-up PR referenced).
- Product: consider a pool-level "small-stream optimized" configuration that prefers larger batching windows and allocation pooling.
- Support: schedule a customer-facing call to walk through connection best practices and collect request samples (requested).

Resolution notes (ongoing):
- Status: mitigation improved latency but not fully resolved; root cause suspected to be combination of coldstart-flood and autoscaler allocation granularity. A permanent fix requires autoscaler tuning and a customer-side client change or a new product knob.
